title: I Built a Personal AI Agent on a Raspberry Pi — Jeremy Adams, Neo4j
talk_summary: Jeremy Adams demos a personal agent running on a Raspberry Pi 4B using NanoClaw (a compact ~15-file OpenClaw alternative) with Docker-isolated agent processes, WhatsApp as the chat channel, cloud LLM inference, and Neo4j for agent memory via MCP. The talk is mostly a hobbyist demo of graph-based memory (P-O-L-E schema) and an offline-capable booth-recording gadget, not a production multi-agent system.

takeaways.technique: Container-per-agent isolation in a minimal orchestrator
takeaways.what_they_do: Chose NanoClaw specifically because it is ~15 source files and runs each agent process in a Docker container so agents cannot run amok on the host.
takeaways.evidence_quote: It just used Docker containers to run the agent processes. So they couldn't run a mock on the system.

takeaways.technique: Graph memory with a fixed entity schema (person/object/location/event/org)
takeaways.what_they_do: Stores agent memories as typed nodes and relationships in Neo4j using a P-O-L-E schema, then retrieves them via an MCP server so the agent can query prior context structurally instead of dumping raw history.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a way of doing memory where you just think of like person, object, location, event

takeaways.technique: MCP server as the single memory/data interface
takeaways.what_they_do: Exposes the memory database to the agent through an MCP server, so the agent reads/writes memory through one tool boundary rather than bespoke integrations.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they're all distilled out into memories that are now accessible via an MCPU server from this very claw

takeaways.technique: Prefer small hackable orchestrators over feature-rich ones
takeaways.what_they_do: Deliberately picked a minimal orchestrator he could read and modify over a popular pre-packaged one, prioritizing understanding over features.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I wanted to understand what was happening more than it being featurerich
